theme: Ruth’s loyalty; arriving in Bethlehem; Boaz introduced
readingInstruction: Read Ruth 1:1-2:23. After the darkness of Judges, the book of Ruth is a bright point of light. The story begins with famine and death, and ends with a field of barley and a kind landowner. Read it as a short story, paying attention to the characters and to the quiet working of God’s providence.
settingTheScene: The book of Ruth is set “in the days when the judges ruled.” This is the same dark era, and yet the story is of ordinary faithfulness. A family from Bethlehem, whose name means “house of bread,” leaves because of a famine and goes to Moab. There, the father and both sons die, leaving three widows. Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem, and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her. The two women arrive in Bethlehem as the barley harvest begins. By chapter 2, Ruth is gleaning in the field of a man named Boaz. The narrator is quietly showing that even in the worst of times, God has not abandoned his people, and that he is working through unnoticed lives.
observation: Elimelech, Naomi, and their two sons leave Bethlehem for Moab because of famine (1:1-2).
Elimelech dies, and the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and then die too (1:3-5).
Naomi hears that “the LORD had visited his people and given them food” and decides to return (1:6-7).
Orpah turns back, but Ruth clings to Naomi: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (1:14-17).
Naomi tells the women of Bethlehem, “Call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me” (1:20).
They arrive “at the beginning of barley harvest” (1:22).
Ruth goes to glean and “happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz” (2:3).
Boaz says, “The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge” (2:12).
Naomi says Boaz is “one of our redeemers” (2:20).
interpretation:
The book opens with sorrow. A family leaves the land of promise for the land of Moab, a nation with a bitter history with Israel. The move seems rational, since there is food in Moab, but it leads to loss. In ten years, Naomi loses her husband and both sons. She returns to Bethlehem with nothing, convinced that the LORD has turned against her. “The hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” Her grief is real, and the text does not scold her. But the narrator slips in a quiet word: Ruth is with her.

Ruth’s vow is among the most famous speeches in the Bible. She is a Moabite, an outsider, with every reason to go home. Naomi tells her twice to leave. Instead she says, “Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.” It is a statement of covenant commitment, not only to a mother-in-law but to the God of Israel. Ruth has chosen to take refuge under the wings of the LORD. Like Rahab, she is a Gentile who joins the people of God by faith. The contrast with Orpah is instructive. Orpah’s decision is not evil, but it is the choice of the familiar. Ruth leaps into the unknown.

The return to Bethlehem is accompanied by honest grief. Naomi says to call her “Mara,” bitter. She says she went away full and has returned empty. But she is wrong on one count: she has Ruth, and the harvest has begun. The narrator marks the timing: “at the beginning of barley harvest.” God is already providing.

Chapter 2 introduces Boaz through a series of coincidences. Ruth “happened” to come to Boaz’s field. This is the narrator’s way of saying that God’s providence is at work in ordinary events, without any miracle. Boaz is generous. He notices Ruth, protects her, tells her to drink from the workers’ water jars, and makes sure extra grain is left for her. He has heard of her loyalty, and he asks that she be rewarded by the God “under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” His blessing is also an unwitting prayer for himself, since he will become the answer to it.

Naomi’s response is a turning point. When she hears that Ruth was in Boaz’s field, her tone shifts: “Blessed be he by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!” She sees that God has not forgotten her. And she identifies Boaz as one of their “redeemers,” a close relative who has the right and duty to restore a family’s fortunes. This is the hinge of the story. The word “redeemer” will carry the book to its conclusion and ultimately to Christ.
connection: Moab’s history with Israel is in Genesis 19:30-38, Numbers 22-25, and Deuteronomy 23:3-6. Ruth’s loyalty parallels Abraham’s call in Genesis 12. The gleaning laws are in Leviticus 19:9-10 and 23:22. The “wings” image is in Psalm 91:4 and Psalm 36:7. The Redeemer language appears in Leviticus 25:25 and Isaiah 41:14. Ruth is named in Matthew 1:5. Bethlehem anticipates Micah 5:2 and Luke 2:4-7.
application:
First, if you are in a season that feels like Naomi’s, empty or bitter, be honest with God, but watch for the signs of his provision. The barley harvest was already beginning. Write down three ways you have seen his kindness in the last month.

Second, learn from Ruth’s loyalty. Is there a person in your life who needs someone to stay beside them? Choose one way to show loyal love this week.

Third, look for the “Boaz” in your community. Kind and generous people are signs of God’s care. Thank one of them today.

Finally, remember that you too have come to take refuge under the wings of the LORD, and the one under whose wings you shelter is Christ.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he works in quiet ways even in dark times.
Ask him to open your eyes to his provision when you feel empty.
Ask him to teach you to take refuge under his wings.
